label: Clinical safety case
title: The product affects “{anchor}”, but no clinical safety assessment or hazard log is referenced
why: Health software can harm patients through wrong, late or missing information. Regulators and hospital buyers expect a documented hazard analysis.
question: Who has assessed the clinical hazards around “{anchor}”, and where is the hazard log?
nextStep: Start a hazard log now and agree the clinical safety sign-off owner.
disproof: A clinical safety case, hazard log or risk-management file.

justifications.cost: Needs clinical input but is well-defined

label: Patient data consent and privacy
title: The documents mention “{anchor}”, but consent, anonymisation and access rules are not described
why: Health data has the strictest privacy rules. Consent gaps can invalidate data collected and block use in research or sales.
question: What consent covers the “{anchor}”, who can access it, and how is it de-identified for secondary use?
nextStep: Document the consent model and access roles, and review them with legal before collecting data.
disproof: A consent, anonymisation or data-protection section covering “{anchor}”.

justifications.impact: Legal exposure and loss of trust
justifications.irreversibility: Data collected without consent may have to be deleted

label: Regulatory approval pathway
title: The product is positioned for “{anchor}”, but no regulatory classification or approval path is stated
why: Regulatory approval can take longer than development and dictates documentation from day one.
question: Which regulatory class applies to “{anchor}” and what is the approval timeline against the launch date?
nextStep: Confirm the classification with a regulatory specialist and add approval milestones to the plan.
disproof: A regulatory classification, approval plan or submission timeline.

justifications.irreversibility: Re-design to meet classification is costly

label: System interoperability
title: Integration with “{anchor}” is assumed, but no interface standard or agreement is mentioned
why: Hospital systems rarely integrate cleanly. Unplanned interface work is a common source of delay.
question: Which interface standard and owner cover the “{anchor}” integration, and has the other side agreed?
nextStep: Get written interface specifications and a named technical contact from the other system.
disproof: An interface specification, standard (HL7/FHIR) or integration agreement for “{anchor}”.

label: Downtime procedures
title: Use in “{anchor}” is planned, but no downtime or manual fallback procedure is described
why: Clinical work cannot stop when software does. Teams need a rehearsed manual process.
question: What do staff in “{anchor}” do when the system is unavailable, and have they practised it?
nextStep: Write a one-page downtime procedure and rehearse it before go-live.
disproof: A downtime, fallback or business-continuity procedure.

justifications.irreversibility: Incidents during downtime cannot be undone

label: Clinician training and adoption

why: Clinicians have little time for new tools. Without training and local champions, usage drops and workarounds appear.
question: How will “{anchor}” be trained, and who supports them on the ward in the first weeks?
